title: Malware check ignores UV_SYSTEM_CERTS / SSL_CERT_FILE — fails with UnknownIssuer behind a TLS-inspecting proxy
body:
### Summary

With the experimental malware check enabled (`UV_MALWARE_CHECK=1`, `--preview-features malware-check`), `uv sync` fails the OSV request to `api.osv.dev` with `invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer` behind a corporate TLS-inspection proxy — **even though a custom root CA is in the system trust store and `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true` (and `SSL_CERT_FILE`) are set.** Package/index downloads through the same proxy work; only the malware-check request fails. This suggests the malware-check HTTP client doesn't use the system / native certificate store.

### uv version

`uv 0.11.21`

### Platform

Linux (Debian 13), building behind a proxy that re-signs TLS with a corporate root.

### Reproduction

Behind a proxy that re-signs TLS with a corporate root (here `CN=httpsinspection.fi.se`):

```console
# corp root installed into the system store
$ update-ca-certificates
$ export UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
$ export UV_MALWARE_CHECK=1 UV_PREVIEW_FEATURES=malware-check
$ uv sync --frozen
error: Malware check failed due to an error from OSV
  Caused by: Request failed after 3 retries
  Caused by: error sending request for url (https://api.osv.dev/v1/querybatch)
  Caused by: client error (Connect)
  Caused by: invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer
```

The same chain validates fine via the system store outside uv:

```console
$ curl https://api.osv.dev/v1/querybatch          # HTTP 405, TLS handshake OK
$ openssl s_client -connect api.osv.dev:443 -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt </dev/null
# ... SSL certificate verify ok.  issuer: CN=httpsinspection.fi.se
```

So the corporate root in the system store *is* trusted by openssl/curl; only uv's malware-check request rejects it.

### Workaround

```console
$ uv sync --allow-insecure-host api.osv.dev    # skips TLS verification for OSV only
```

### Expected behavior

The malware check should honor `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` / `SSL_CERT_FILE` (and the system trust store) the same way package/index downloads do, so it works behind a TLS-inspecting proxy without disabling certificate verification for `api.osv.dev`.

comments.author: user-7f2a9b1f4e
user-7f2a9b1f4e
comments.body:
Confirming this is the malware-check client ignoring the trust store, **not** a cert/config problem on our side:

- The proxy re-signs `api.osv.dev` with a self-signed corporate root (`CN=httpsinspection.fi.se`). That exact root is installed in the image's system store via `update-ca-certificates`, and `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true` + `SSL_CERT_FILE` are set.
- The bundled root **matches the live proxy root byte-for-byte** — same subject and identical validity window (`notBefore=2024-01-01 10:09:41Z`, `notAfter=2030-04-09 10:19:41Z`), verified against `openssl s_client`/`curl` output.
- `openssl`/`curl` (using that system store) validate `api.osv.dev` fine, and uv's **package/index downloads through the same proxy succeed** — only the malware-check request to `api.osv.dev` fails with `UnknownIssuer`.

So the system store contains the correct, in-date root and is honored everywhere except the malware check. `--allow-insecure-host api.osv.dev` is the only thing that lets the malware check proceed behind the inspecting proxy. It'd be great if the malware-check HTTP client used the same TLS/cert configuration (`UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` / `SSL_CERT_FILE`) as the rest of uv.

Further confirmation that the OSV request itself works through the inspecting proxy — it's specifically uv's malware-check HTTP client that refuses it.

Replaying uv's exact malware-check request with `curl` (which uses the system trust store) through the **same** TLS-inspection proxy succeeds:

```console
$ curl -X POST https://api.osv.dev/v1/querybatch \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"queries":[{"package":{"name":"requests","ecosystem":"PyPI"},"version":"2.34.2"}]}'
{"results":[{}]}
```

Same host and proxy-resigned cert (`issuer: CN=httpsinspection.fi.se`, `verify ok`) that uv's malware check rejects with `UnknownIssuer`. uv's package/index downloads through this proxy also succeed. So the only component not honoring `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` / `SSL_CERT_FILE` / the system trust store is the malware-check client.

comments.author: user-4658b24f09
comments.body:
I'm having some trouble reproducing this: our construction of the HTTP client for the OSV lookup goes through our normal client building machinery, which has the `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` and `SSL_CERT_FILE` states propagated into it. So the problem isn't those being ignored, but something else about your TLS stack or certificate bundle.

(curl is a red herring here, since it almost certainly uses a totally different TLS stack than uv, even if it uses the same certificate bundle.)

Some things that would help us better understand the underlying problem here:

- Try re-running with verbose logs, e.g. `UV_MALWARE_CHECK=1 UV_PREVIEW_FEATURES=malware-check uv -vv sync` and share those logs with us.
- Try running `openssl s_client -showcerts api.osv.dev:443` and share that output with us. That'll show us what constructed chain OpenSSL is actually using, which might help us determine any divergences versus rustls-webpki.

(Separately, you really only need one of `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` or `SSL_CERT_FILE` -- uv always prefers the latter if both are set, so setting both has no effect.)

comments.author: user-7f2a9b1f4e
comments.body:
Closing this — after more digging I can't substantiate it as a uv defect, and I don't want to leave a misleading report.

What we actually established in our setup (DHI Python Debian 13, behind a corporate TLS-inspection proxy):

- The corporate root **was** installed and trusted by the OpenSSL-based tools (`curl`, `apt`) via `update-ca-certificates` — those validated the proxy-resigned certs fine.
- We could not get uv to validate the same certs via `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS` / `SSL_CERT_FILE`, **but** we never isolated a clean minimal reproduction proving uv ignores a correctly-configured store. Our cert wiring on the hardened image was in flux, and one of our own changes briefly corrupted the CA bundle — so the earlier "package downloads work, only the malware check fails" comparison was not sound (downloads were served from uv's cache).
- We resolved it on our side with `--allow-insecure-host pypi.org files.pythonhosted.org api.osv.dev`. That's safe for us because `uv.lock` is fully hashed and `--frozen` verifies every artifact's sha256 (integrity is independent of TLS), and the inspecting proxy already terminates TLS.

So this is most likely a configuration issue on our end on a hardened base, not a uv bug. Apologies for the noise. If I later get a clean, minimal reproduction that uv ignores a properly-installed system store / `SSL_CERT_FILE` while OpenSSL tools accept it, I'll open a fresh issue with exact steps.

body:
### Summary

Thank you for the fantastic job on **uv** and Astral's other projects!

I manage a private, workspace-enabled project. Workspace members rely on the **hatchling** build backend. Builds are performed on AWS CodeBuild using AWS CodeArtifact as a private package index, which is configured via the `UV_DEFAULT_INDEX` environment variable. This works flawlessly.

To harden against supply chain risks, I am introducing `exclude-newer = "1 week"` to the `[tool.uv]` section in the root `pyproject.toml`. The lockfile updates as expected, but this currently breaks my CI pipeline: Dependency resolution of the **hatchling** build backend fails:

title: `uv tree`'s --depth behaviour is strange on scripts and workspace-groups
body:
### Summary

An elaboration on more problematic cases alluded to in the second half of https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/19973

`uv tree --depth=0` on a package produces only the package.
`uv tree --depth=0` on a workspace produces a list of workspace members.
`uv tree --depth=0 --script=myscript` produces the direct dependencies of the script
`uv tree --depth=0` on a virtual workspace that defines dependency-groups will produce the contents of the dependency groups (by default just the default groups).

This is inconsistent and weird, I would expect all of them to produce no dependencies. (At best reporting a "script" node or "workspace"/"workspace group" node with no children).


# Workspace Example

(The `tool.uv.workspace` entry here isn't theoretically necessary, but see https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/19975)

```toml
[dependency-groups]
dev = ["flask==3.0.2"]

[tool.uv]
# Keep the transitive versions stable when this demonstration is rerun.
exclude-newer = "2024-03-25T00:00:00Z"

[tool.uv.workspace]
# Make the directory an explicitly virtual workspace without adding a project.
members = []
```

```
uv tree --depth 0

Using CPython 3.14.5
warning: No `requires-python` value found in the workspace. Defaulting to `>=3.14`.
Resolved 8 packages in 3ms
flask v3.0.2 (group: dev)
```

# Script Example

```py
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# dependencies = [
#   "requests==2.31.0",
#   "rich==13.7.1",
# ]
#
# [tool.uv]
# exclude-newer = "2024-03-25T00:00:00Z"
# ///

from importlib.metadata import version

import requests
from rich import print

print(f"[bold green]Success:[/] requests {requests.__version__} and rich {version('rich')} are importable")
```

### Summary

I've noticed that `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` has no corresponding flag ([docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/environment/#uv_prerelease)) to specify it via a flag to the command as e.g. `uv sync --venv <my_env>`.

Perhaps, I could get some time from work to spend on this as we're interested in that feature.

 (I made minor contributions to UV about a year ago but may require some handholding). 

## Context
We're using UV on our slurm clusters usually have a first job that later launches other child or first class jobs. To avoid races on the shared filesystem as well as redundant work, we pre-build the environments of our uv projects running in these jobs. Now we have new nodes with different architectures which sometimes makes using the prebuild envs blow up. We can simply set the environment variable conditionally, but they are propagated to inherting slurm jobs and it would be nicer to also be able to just pass it as a CLI flag. 

Maybe there is also a better way to handle x86 / arm mismatches. Happy for pointers if you have ideas. 

Cheers and thank you for making Python a better place :)

title: adjust-ulimit (0.12.0) makes every tcsh/csh subprocess ~100x slower
body:
### Summary

## Summary

Since uv 0.12.0 stabilized the `adjust-ulimit` behavior (PR #20225), the
raised soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` is inherited by all subprocesses and breaks
tools whose startup cost scales with the open-file limit. In particular,
`tcsh` (`/bin/csh`) closes **every file descriptor from 0 to
`RLIMIT_NOFILE`** at startup, so any csh subprocess under `uv run` pays
O(RLIMIT_NOFILE) syscalls (~524k `close()` calls) and becomes ~100x slower.

This effectively makes `uv run` unusable for csh-based toolchains (e.g. the
GAMIT GNSS processing suite, which is entirely csh scripts).

## Environment

- uv: 0.12.1 (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl), also reproduced reasoning applies to 0.12.0
- Linux container (Debian/Ubuntu base), image built with `COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest`
- `/bin/csh` = tcsh 6.x

## Reproduction

```sh
# NOFILE before uv: soft=1024, hard=524288
python3 -c 'import resource; print(resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE))'
# (1024, 524288)

# After uv: soft raised to hard
uv run python3 -c 'import resource; print(resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE))'
# (524288, 524288)

# Time a trivial csh invocation
time uv run /bin/csh -f -c 'exit 0'        # ~0.37s
time /bin/csh -f -c 'exit 0'               # ~0.002s

# strace shows the child closing the whole fd range:
#   close(39031) close(142232) close(267235) ... close(524287)  (~524,424 calls)
```

With the limit capped, it is fast again:

```sh
ulimit -n 4096 && uv run /bin/csh -f -c 'exit 0'   # ~0.005s
```

Real-world impact: a GAMIT project-setup script (`sh_setup`) takes ~10s
under `uv run` vs ~0.14s with `ulimit -n 1024`.

## Root cause

uv 0.12.0 stabilized "Automatic open-file limit adjustment on Unix"
(#20225, originally #17464): uv raises the soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` toward the
hard limit (capped at 1,048,576) at startup, and the new limit applies to
subprocesses.

`tcsh` (and `csh`) at startup iterate `close()` from 0 to `sysconf(_SC_OPEN_MAX)`
(= soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE`) to prevent leaking inherited file descriptors. With
the soft limit raised to 524288, each csh process executes ~524k `close()`
syscalls. csh-based toolchains chain many such subprocesses, so the cost
compounds.

## Expected behavior

Raising `RLIMIT_NOFILE` is fine for uv itself, but the raised soft limit
being inherited by every subprocess (`exec`ed via `uv run`) has surprising
O(limit) startup costs in otherwise-unaffected tools.

Options to consider:

- Only raise the soft limit for the uv process itself, and restore the
  original soft limit around `uv run` subprocess spawns.
- Respect an existing lower soft limit (don't raise it when the process was
  started under an already-low limit), or make the adjustment opt-out via an
  env var (e.g. `UV_NO_ULIMIT=1`).
- Cap the inherited soft limit for subprocesses lower than uv's own limit.

## Workaround (current)

Wrap `uv run` with a capped limit:

```sh
ulimit -n 4096 && exec uv run ...
```

## Note

`adjust-ulimit` was opt-in (preview) before 0.12.0, so this is a behavior
regression introduced by the 0.12.0 stabilization for any program whose
startup scales with the open-file limit.

### Platform

Linux container (Debian/Ubuntu base)

### Version

0.12.1

### Python version

3.13.6

```
[install]
extra-index-url = <https://pipindex.company.com>

_No response_
author: user-f21845f7e0

comments.author: user-4658b24f09
comments.body: Technically speaking I think we could add this, but I think it might be pretty risky security-wise: `extra-index-url` is discouraged (versus `index-url`) because it composes indices together in a way that enables dependency confusion. Adding support for disabling retries means that a network path attacker can potentially induce that confusion just by inducing a failure, which is a much easier thing for them to do than e.g. perform an active MITM.

comments.author: user-09f6134884
comments.body:
@user-4658b24f09 I wouldn't say `extra-index-url` is discouraged. Our default index strategy is already designed to reduce dependency confusion attacks. I think its fine to use the feature.

I agree however that if the intent is to switch indexes when one is not available, you are exposing yourself to additional risk. Instead, you probably want a feature like we're working on for proxy indexes specifically; see #20790

title: Provide a way to select the interpreter used for venv creation without overriding installation target of `uv pip`
body:
### Summary

Currently, `UV_PYTHON` seems to have basically two distinguishable meanings:

1. Prefer this interpreter when creating a virtual environment
2. Use this interpreter's default environment for `uv pip` operations

. I, as a NixOS user with a OS-managed Python, would love to use `UV_PYTHON` for the first, but never the second.

Now I need to take care to set `UV_PYTHON` only for operations that create virtual environments and unset it for other operations.

I think a useful and backwards compatible model could be something like:

- Have `UV_PYTHON` behave exactly as it does currently
- Introduce a new environment variable `UV_BASE_PYTHON`, with the semantics of only affecting interpreter choice when creating a new venv, but not other uv operations.

### Example

Consider this behavior:

```
$ echo $UV_PYTHON
/nix/store/gxzhl7aaiid7zp3y47jqqiq7zg5mqpwp-python3-3.14.6/bin/python

$ uv venv new-venv
Using CPython 3.14.6 interpreter at: /nix/store/gxzhl7aaiid7zp3y47jqqiq7zg5mqpwp-python3-3.14.6/bin/python
Creating virtual environment at: new-venv
Activate with: source new-venv/bin/activate

$ source new-venv/bin/activate

(new-venv)
$ uv pip install setuptools
Using Python 3.14.6 environment at: /nix/store/gxzhl7aaiid7zp3y47jqqiq7zg5mqpwp-python3-3.14.6
error: The interpreter at /nix/store/gxzhl7aaiid7zp3y47jqqiq7zg5mqpwp-python3-3.14.6 is externally managed, and indicates the following:

  This command has been disabled as it tries to modify the immutable
  `/nix/store` filesystem.

  To use Python with Nix and nixpkgs, have a look at the online documentation:
  <https://nixos.org/manual/nixpkgs/stable/

hint: Consider creating a virtual environment, e.g., with `uv venv`

$
```

The `uv venv` command did what I wanted. However, `uv pip install` did not (IIUC https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/6612 is a discussion related to this, but, also IIUC, not quite the same thing).

Instead, with my proposed `UV_BASE_PYTHON` this could look like this: 

```
$ echo $UV_PYTHON

$ echo $UV_BASE_PYTHON
/nix/store/gxzhl7aaiid7zp3y47jqqiq7zg5mqpwp-python3-3.14.6/bin/python

Using CPython 3.14.6 interpreter at: /nix/store/gxzhl7aaiid7zp3y47jqqiq7zg5mqpwp-python3-3.14.6/bin/python
Creating virtual environment at: new-venv
Activate with: source new-venv/bin/activate

$ source new-venv/bin/activate

(new-venv)

```

title: Command to verify uv.lock is legitimate
body:
### Summary

Currently, there seems to be no way to verify that a uv.lock has not maliciously been tampered with. It would be nice if this can be automatically checked, because manually verifying lock file changes is error-prone and likely often neglected (even the github UI hides uv.lock diffs per default).

I would like to have a command (part of `uv sync`, `uv lock` or `uv audit`) that checks if the dependencies in uv.lock match the definitions in pyproject.toml. I think this would require fetching the metadata again from PyPi.

This is to prevent against this scenario:
- some creates a malicious PR: pyproject.toml looks good (only pytest is updated); uv.lock has legitimate updates + a single wheel url has been changed to point to the attacker-controlled domain pythonhcsted instead of pythonhosted
- maintainer looks at the PR:
- - either only verifies the pyproject.toml diff. Easy and short to verify
- - or even expands the uv.lock diff and needs a lot of luck to find the difference between `pythonhcsted` and `pythonhosted` (`c` vs `o`)

It seems that the only safe way to handle PRs that add lines to uv.lock files is to close them, because I have no way to tell if there is a security issue hidden inside. I'd like that to be different, and also I guess many maintainers are not aware of this.

This issue is not unique to uv. For instance, here is an article describing malicious package-lock.json changes in npm: https://snyk.io/blog/why-npm-lockfiles-can-be-a-security-blindspot-for-injecting-malicious-modules/

### Example

I lack the knowledge how exactly things work in the background, but from a high level point of view I want something like this:

```bash
uv lock --verify
# check that there are no unexpected dependencies in `uv.lock` that are neither declared in pyproject.toml nor are they transitive dependencies
# verify that uv.lock versions are within the version ranges of pyproject.toml
# verify that sdist and wheel urls point to the urls described by the index in pyproject.toml
```

From a quick check, `Lock::satisfies` checks if the lockfile still matches the project inputs and configuration. Registry packages are marked as immutable by `is_immutable` which causes per-package validation (including dependency traversal from that package) to be skipped. If the resulting check does succeed the `do_lock` returns `LockResult::Unchanged` without doing a fresh resolution.

title: `uv lock` scales exponentially with the size of a single `[tool.uv] conflicts` group
body:
### Summary

`uv lock` time grows exponentially with the number of extras declared mutually-exclusive in one `[tool.uv] conflicts` group — but only when the project also has a dependency shared across those forks with a large release history (e.g. `transformers`). It roughly doubles every 5-10 extras (24s at N=50 → 110s at N=65), and past a threshold (~70 in the minimal repro below) it no longer completes within any reasonable time.


### Minimal reproduction

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# repro.sh - for each N, generates a pyproject.toml with N empty extras all
# declared mutually exclusive in one [tool.uv] conflicts group, plus one real
# dependency (transformers, chosen for its large release history), and times
# `uv lock`. Prints the full table from this report.
set -euo pipefail
TIMEOUT_S="${TIMEOUT_S:-120}"

gen_pyproject() {
  local n="$1" workdir="$2"
  {
    echo '[project]'
    echo 'name = "repro"'
    echo 'version = "0.0.1"'
    echo 'requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.15"'
    echo 'dependencies = ["transformers>=4.40.0,<6.0.0"]'
    echo
    echo '[project.optional-dependencies]'
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do echo "e${i} = []"; done
    echo
    echo '[tool.uv]'
    printf 'conflicts = [\n    ['
    for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do
      printf '{ extra = "e%d" }' "$i"
      [ "$i" -lt $((n - 1)) ] && printf ', '
    done
    printf '],\n]\n'
  } > "$workdir/pyproject.toml"
}

echo "uv: $(uv --version)"
echo

for n in 5 10 20 30 40 50 55 60 65 70 80 90; do
  workdir="$(mktemp -d -t uv-conflicts-repro-XXXXXX)"
  gen_pyproject "$n" "$workdir"
  start=$(date +%s.%N)
  if timeout "$TIMEOUT_S" uv lock --project "$workdir" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    outcome="resolved"
  else
    [ $? -eq 124 ] && outcome="TIMEOUT(${TIMEOUT_S}s)" || outcome="error"
  fi
  end=$(date +%s.%N)
  elapsed=$(awk "BEGIN { printf \"%.1f\", $end - $start }")
  printf 'n=%-4s  %-16s  %6ss\n' "$n" "$outcome" "$elapsed"
  rm -rf "$workdir"
done
```

```bash
chmod +x repro.sh
./repro.sh
```

### Timings

| N extras in the group | time |
|---|---|
| 5 | 0.0s |
| 10 | 0.0s |
| 20 | 0.2s |
| 30 | 1.2s |
| 40 | 6.5s |
| 50 | 23.4s |
| 55 | 41.0s |
| 60 | 70.7s |
| 65 | 109.9s |
| 70 | doesn't finish within 120s |
| 80 | doesn't finish within 120s |
| 90 | doesn't finish within 120s |

Grouping shape: splitting the same total extras into many small *disjoint* `conflicts` groups performs identically to one big group — it's the total distinct extra count across `conflicts`, not group size or group count, that predicts the time.

### Context

Found while investigating `uv lock` runs that took multiple hours on [embeddings-benchmark/mteb](https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb) — one run [wasn't finished after 12 hours](https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb/issues/5482) and had to be killed. mteb declares ~44 extras mutually exclusive in one group alongside `transformers`/`torch`/`sentence-transformers` as base deps (their real threshold was ~40, lower than this single-dependency repro's ~65 — consistent with multiple large-history deps compounding).

### Related issues

- **#21399**: same *kind* of fix, but scoped to workspaces with many member projects — doesn't cover a single project's own `conflicts` group.
- **#18317**: lock file size scaling with `conflicts`.
- **#17990**: asks for conflicting groups to resolve as independent targets instead of one universal resolution — would likely fix this too.
- **https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16779**: Similar problem


### Platform

\macOS 27.0 arm64

### Version

uv 0.12.17

### Python version

_No response_

body:
### Summary

When running [uv-installer.ps1](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/download/0.12.23/uv-installer.ps1) in Windows with `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` environment variables used:

- NO_PROXY value is discarded.

This is an issue for my organisation, as internal assets cannot be accessed through the proxy, and we use an internal mirror for `UV_INSTALLER_GITHUB_BASE_URL`.

The part that fails is:
`function WebProxyFromEnvironment {
    $httpsProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("HTTPS_PROXY")
    $allProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("ALL_PROXY")
    $proxyUrl = if (-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($httpsProxy)) { $httpsProxy } else { $allProxy }
    $webProxy = WebProxyFromUrl -ProxyUrl $proxyUrl
    return $webProxy
}`

One correction could be (maybe with added null check):
`function WebProxyFromEnvironment {
    $httpsProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("HTTPS_PROXY")
    $allProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("ALL_PROXY")
    $noProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("NO_PROXY")
    $proxyUrl = if (-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($httpsProxy)) { $httpsProxy } else { $allProxy }
    $webProxy = WebProxyFromUrl -ProxyUrl $proxyUrl -BypassList $noProxy
    return $webProxy
}`

title: `uv build --all-packages` deadlocks with a cold cache: wheel-lock waiters exhaust the tokio blocking pool
body:
### Summary

`uv build --all-packages` on a large workspace (54 members, all `hatchling` + `hatch-vcs`) intermittently hangs forever when the cache is cold (`UV_NO_CACHE=1`, or a fresh `UV_CACHE_DIR`). uv never spawns a build backend, and the 5-minute `UV_LOCK_TIMEOUT` default does not fire. In CI the hang lasts until the 6h job timeout.

### Observations (uv 0.12.23, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

- All 54 `[pkg] Building source distribution...` lines print, then nothing. The `uv` process has **0 child processes**.
- `-v` logs 530 `INFO Waiting to acquire exclusive lock for .../wheels-v6/pypi/<build-req>/<version>-py3-none-any.lock` lines within the same second. They cover the ~10 shared build requirements (hatchling, hatch-vcs, setuptools-scm, vcs-versioning, packaging, pathspec, pluggy, trove-classifiers, setuptools, tomlkit), ~53 waiters each.
- The process sits at **514 threads**, with ~541 open `.lock` fds and 11 flocks held by the same pid (`/proc/locks`). These numbers don't change for more than 6 minutes, and no lock-timeout error is ever printed.

### Likely mechanism

`LockedFile::lock_file` (`crates/uv-fs/src/locked_file.rs`) waits for a contended lock with `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || mode.lock(&file))`, which is a blocking `flock` on the blocking pool (default cap 512). `lock_wheel` (`crates/uv-distribution/src/distribution_database.rs`) holds the wheel-cache lock across download and extraction, and extraction also runs on the blocking pool. Once the waiters (54 builds × ~10 shared build requirements ≈ 540) occupy all 512 blocking threads, the lock holders' extraction work is queued behind them and never runs, so the locks are never released.

The `tokio::time::timeout(*LOCK_TIMEOUT, …)` around the waiter also doesn't seem to rescue this. A waiter that times out still leaves its blocking thread parked in `flock`, and the holders (which have no timeout) keep the overall build pending.

### Reproduction sketch

1. A workspace with ~50+ members, each with `[build-system] requires = ["hatchling", "hatch-vcs"]`.
2. `UV_NO_CACHE=1 uv build --all-packages --out-dir dist/`

The hang is timing-dependent: a few percent of runs on a 4-vCPU CI runner, and nearly every run on a heavily loaded 4-core host.

### Workaround

Building members in separate processes with bounded parallelism (`uv workspace list --paths | xargs -P4 -I{} uv build {} --out-dir dist/`, sharing one cache) avoids the hang.

### Suggestions

- Wait for contended locks without parking a blocking-pool thread per waiter, for example by polling `try_lock` with backoff, or by deduplicating in-process waiters on the same path with an async mutex before taking the flock.
- And/or bound concurrent build-environment setup so that waiters can't exceed the blocking pool.
